title: Nuclear Semiotics: How to Talk to Future Humans
summary: Josh and Chuck explore nuclear semiotics: how to warn people thousands to hundreds of thousands of years in the future about buried nuclear waste. They cover the rationale for deep geological repositories in salt beds, why language and symbols won't last, the history of the nuclear trefoil symbol, and the 1980s Human Interference Task Force and Yucca Mountain work. They discuss ideas like glowing yucca plants, screeching blades, razor wire, an atomic priesthood, and the meta message, and then the WIPP (Waste Isolation Pilot Plant) in New Mexico, whose final marker design includes an earthen berm, granite monoliths with warnings in seven languages, and a human-pain pictogram influenced by Edvard Munch's The Scream. The episode closes with Sweden's Forsmark application, a Josh plug for The End of the World, and a listener mail.

The End of the World with Josh Clark

segments.title: Opening banter and live show dates
segments.summary: Hosts flub the intro, discuss recent live shows in Chicago and Toronto and upcoming dates including Portland, Maine, and introduce the nuclear semiotics topic, noting the Visible episode on it.

segments.title: Why warn the future about nuclear waste
segments.summary: Definition of nuclear semiotics and the challenge of warning future humans. Discussion of waste half-lives (plutonium-239, technetium-99) and how languages and symbols may not survive.

segments.title: Deep geological repositories and salt beds
segments.summary: Explains long-term geological repositories dug miles into the earth, why salt beds are preferred (no water, easy to mine, salt heals over), and the responsibility to warn the future rather than simply bury and forget. Percy Tannenbaum's suggestion to leave the site unmarked is mentioned.

segments.title: WIPP in New Mexico and the origins of the field
segments.summary: WIPP is the only operating US repository, with the Department of Energy committed to guarding it for at least 100 years. Yucca Mountain in Nevada was the earlier, never-completed project. The EPA rule requiring a permanent warning marker led to the discipline taking shape around 1981.

segments.title: History and design of the nuclear trefoil symbol
segments.summary: The trefoil began as a 1946 group doodle at Berkeley and was standardized for Brookhaven National Laboratory, with colors debated. Magenta on blue was the original design; Oak Ridge National Laboratory later used yellow. The hosts note the symbol is not universally understood and would not evoke an atom in the distant future.

segments.title: Language extinction and the limits of text warnings
segments.summary: Languages die out at a rate of roughly one every two weeks. English changes quickly, illustrated by a passage from Sir Gawain and the Green Knight. Instant recognition and emotional warnings are favored, but a fine line exists between warning and enticing people, as with haunted houses and extreme sports.
topics: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight

segments.title: Semiotics basics and the glowing yucca and competition ideas
segments.summary: Semiotics defined as the study of how signs carry meaning. The Desert Space Competition at UCLA in 2001 produced ideas such as genetically engineered glowing yucca plants; the hosts critique the need for added explanation. Fields of Asphodel's screeching metal blades were rejected due to moving parts, and razor wire was dismissed because people would scavenge useful materials.

segments.title: Atomic priesthood, meta message, and the WIPP marker plan
segments.summary: Thomas Sebeok's ideas include a fake atomic priesthood (criticized as despicable) and the meta message, a translatable warning kept alongside the original. Long-term communication has direct and successive forms. Skull and crossbones was proposed by Carl Sagan but rejected by the working group as culturally limited. The hosts discuss the WIPP design: a field of spikes, a disk painted as a black hole, pictograms of human agony inspired by Edvard Munch's The Scream, and a trefoil berm with granite slabs in seven languages with blank spaces for future translations.

segments.title: Space disposal, Sweden's application, and closing thoughts
segments.summary: Shooting waste into space is discussed as a risky idea. Sweden's Forsmark application deferred documentation for seventy years, which the Swedish National Archives criticized. Lomberg's comments about the US effort are noted. Josh plugs The End of the World with Josh Clark.
topics: The End of the World podcast

segments.title: Listener mail from Kate
segments.summary: A listener named Kate, an English teacher who moved from Phoenix to Charlotte after a breakup, thanks the hosts for getting her through the drive while listening to the show, and says her brother Nick became a fan.
